newsitem.title: USA: FAA awards $1 billion contract to Raytheon team.
newsitem.headline: FAA awards $1 billion contract to Raytheon team.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration said Monday it awarded a contract potentially worth nearly $1 billion to a team of companies led by Raytheon Co. to upgrade air traffic control systems.
Raytheon won the contract over rival bidders Boeing Co. and Lockheed Martin Corp. because of the technology portion of its proposal, FAA officials said.

The contract is to build the Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System, or STARS, to replace air traffic control computers with a next-generation system for FAA and Department of Defence facilities across the country. The systems are used in the airspace within about 50 miles of airports.

Raytheon will provide systems and services necessary to develop, integrate and install new traffic computers, displays and software in Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities and towers, the FAA said in a statement.
"It will provide air traffic controllers with the very latest in technology, replacing 20-year-old equipment," Transportation Secretary Federico Pena said.
"Consumers will see fewer delays, systems will be safer, more reliable, and will grow as traffic grows over the next several decades," he told reporters at a briefing.
Travel on U.S. airlines is expected to grow to nearly 800 million people by 2003 from about 580 million in 1995, the FAA said.
STARS will put in place the latest aircraft radar display equipment at 172 FAA control facilities and towers and in 199 Defence Department military facilities.
The FAA said it planned to have the first STARS operational in Boston by December 1998, with subsequent deliveries to FAA and Defence facilities through 2007.
"The new radar displays will replace 20-year-old terminals that controllers now use with larger, easier to see full-colour, digitized displays," Pena said.
Additional information such as weather reports will also appear on the new displays.

Bids submitted by the three companies vying for the contract were close, within a few percentage points, and in this case "technical won out," said David Ford, leader of the FAA's terminal integrated product team, which was responsible for choosing the contractor.
Raytheon's equipment division in Marlborough, Mass., will lead a team to build STARS.

Other members of the Raytheon team include General Motors Corp. units Hughes Information Systems of Fullerton, Calif.; Magnavox Electronic Systems Co. of Fort Wayne, Ind.; Sun Microsystems Federal Inc. of Mountainview, Calif.; and UFA Inc. of Lexington, Mass.
Lexington, Mass.-based Raytheon's stock rose 50 cents to $52 and GM climbed $1.125 to $50.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late morning trading. Sun Micro rose 25 cents to $57.25 on Nasdaq.
